articles.headline: Freighting.
articles.text: The building of railroads into the western states and territories is rapidly driving the old time bull and mule outfits out of existence and causing at the same time a feeling of dismay in the heart of the true frontiersman, to whom the crack of the bull whips and stentorian tones of the bull-whacker and mule-skinner are music sweet to hear, because the points to and from which freight is hauled are always lively and hard times never known. Many towns on the Missouri, Platte, Smoky Hill and Arkansas rivers have been virtually built and sustained to a great extent by the old time freighters, who are as a class jovial, generous and extravagant to a fault, who spend their earnings with a lavish hand. In the northwest particularly is this fact noticeable, and when we note all that the freight business has done for Cheyenne, Sidney and Pierre, now right at the present time, before it is too late, the importance of doing all in our power to make Medora a permanent starting point for Black Hills freight presents itself. It can only be for a comparatively short time that any of the present starting points for Black Hills freight can reap the harvest from this industry, because in the near future no less than four railroads will be building towards that Eden of America, therefore the present time is the season for extending every effort and using every influence with the railroad company, the shippers and the freighters to have this point designated as the only one on this line to which Black Hills freight can be consigned. We have such natural advantages as cannot be overlooked either by the railroad officials or freighters, the road is undoubtedly the best ever traveled over by freight teams, better time is made loaded or empty than on the Pierre road, the distance is shorter than that route, instead of traveling over nearly 200 miles of gumbo belt this route only crosses the belt a distance of 33 miles. With these advantages in our favor the course to pursue is patent to any man. Let the railroad company, instead of giving special rates to any point and to any man who may ask it, make a contract with one reliable forwarding company and to this one point. This will encourage the shippers in the Hills, because then they will know exactly what course to pursue and where to look for their freight and to whom to look for damages in case of delay or carelessness, and besides such a course will give full satisfaction to the freighters who to day cannot tell whether to come to Medora, Dickinson or Belfield for freight. The Black Hills freight this year will amount in the aggregate to at least 15,000,000 pounds, and during this month, August and September will the large proportion of this amount be shipped, and right now is the time for all concerned to figure. The most of this freight is shipped in carload lots, and consequently the railroad company can afford to give good rates, the freighters hauling for $1.65 a hundred, are working fully as cheap as they can. If the Northern Pacific railroad wants the Black Hills freight it can undoubtedly get more than a fair proportion, but the forwarding company must be protected by contract and thereby be enabled to protect the teamsters, who will then know from whom and where to make sure of a load. Under the present management apparently no one knows when he can get loaded or where he can load from, and this uncertainty will in the end not only work hardship on the freighter but drive him to other routes where he knows such contracts exist between the railroad and forwarding companies as enable the latter to be always able to tell to within a few days of the time of the arrival of freight. We predict that if such steps are not taken the shippers and freighters will get so disgusted that the railroad will lose this freight entirely.
articles.summary: Editorial urging that Medora be made the sole Northern Pacific starting point for Black Hills freight, under a contract with one forwarding company.

articles.headline: The Governorship.
articles.text:
Col. G. A. Pierce, of Chicago, has been appointed governor of Dakota, vice Ordway, whose term has expired. It has been known for some time that the administration was decidedly opposed to the appointment of any Dakota candidate for this position, for the reason that all prominent Dakota men were supposed to be interested on one side or the other of the capital question, and the appointment of any Dakota man would have placed the administration apparently in the position of bolstering up one side or the other in the Dakota controversy. To preserve neutrality Mr. Ordway was suffered to serve his term, and continued until all legal proceedings against him were disposed of, and then one who has not the slightest interest in either faction was appointed as his successor.—[Bismarck Journal.

In making this appointment the president has made a wise choice. From personal knowledge we predict without fear of contradiction that Col. Pierce will make the best governor this territory has ever had.—[Ed.
articles.summary: Bismarck Journal report of Col. G. A. Pierce's appointment as governor of Dakota in place of Ordway, with the editor's endorsement of Pierce.

articles.text:
The parties who control the ranching business in the Yellowstone region give public notice that there is no room for more ranges and that in the future they will not allow any new comers the privileges of the round-up.[—Western Central Kansas Cow Boy.

The above was evidently written by some tenderfoot with an idea that such a report would cause stockmen to refrain from driving into these ranges. It is too ridiculous to even need contradiction, for every cattle man knows that no such action as barring owners from the privileges of the round-up would be to tolerated on any range. As to the statement that the Yellowstone range is crowded, we do not believe it, but, even if such is a fact, the Bad Lands ranges are not, and to-day no better cattle country can be found in the United States than in these ranges, where there is abundance of water, shelter and feed, and of such quality that cattle are in good beef condition all the year round.—[Ed.
articles.summary: Clipped report that Yellowstone ranchers would bar newcomers from the round-up, with the editor's rebuttal that the Bad Lands ranges are not crowded.

articles.text: At Jacksonville, Ill., June 6th J. H. Potts & Son sold 23 females and 6 bulls for $9,420, average $325. So Shorthorns still sell well.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped note on a Shorthorn sale at Jacksonville, Illinois.

articles.text: An exchange says that more than 375,000 head of young cattle will be driven out of Texas this season, and although this is the largest output in her history, stockmen claim that there will be left in the state more young stock than ever before held over.—[Western Central Kansas Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Clipped note that more than 375,000 young cattle will be driven out of Texas this season.

articles.text: There is no need of bothering about a cow's pulse to find out if she is well or not; simple look at her nose. If well, it will be moist and cold; if feverish, dry and hot. She is like a dog in this respect A staring coat or a hollow eye are also points indicating trouble, and as symptoms of diseases they are more to be dreaded than the dry nose.—[Dairyman.
articles.summary: Clipped hint on judging a cow's health by her nose.

articles.text: The advertising columns of The Bad Lands Cow Boy presents a very unique appearance to the eastern reader. One page contains the announcement of thirty-one brands, ranges, ear mark and vint, and the headquarters of nearly all these ranges are at Medora, in Billings county. It shows how rapidly Dakota is becoming a stock as well as a wheat country.—[Fargo Argus.
articles.summary: The Fargo Argus remarks on the Cow Boy's page of thirty-one cattle-brand advertisements as a sign of Dakota's growth as stock country.

articles.text: The use of blood as food for cattle has, it is stated, been the subject of experiment in Denmark by a chemist, who, as a result, has now invented and patented a new kind of cake in which blood forms one of the chief ingredients. This new food is stated to be exceedingly nutritious and wholesome, and is eaten with avidity by all sorts of animals, and even by cows and horses which have naturally a strong dislike to the smell of blood.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped note on a Danish blood-based cattle feed cake.

articles.text: A cow belonging to Mr. George Markham, of St. Mary's crossing, on the Huerfano, last week gave birth to two calves which are alive and doing well. This is the second or third pair of twins which this cow has given birth to and raised. Moreover, she is herself a twin, her mother also having raised several pairs of twins. Mr. Markham says the Herefords, Shorthorns or Polled Anguses may be very good cattle, but this breed is good enough for him.—[Heurfano Cactus.
articles.summary: Clipped story of a Colorado cow that has raised several pairs of twins.

articles.text: To run the gauntlet of a sojourn among the Texas cowboys; to prove that frequent predictions of broken limbs and a broken neck as the result of too daring horsemanship were ill-founded; and then to break a leg upon the platform of a London railway station on the way from the Derby, is almost a descent from the sublime to the ridiculous. Yet such has been the fate of Lord Aylesford, and his lordship's mishap, for which we are sincerely sorry, might enable an active emigration agent to score one, and point out that Texas, despite its somewhat doubtful reputation, was the safest spot on earth for members of the aristocracy addicted to horse flesh.—[Industrial and Commercial Gazette.
articles.summary: Clipped item on Lord Aylesford breaking a leg in London after surviving life among Texas cowboys.

articles.text: The President having signed the pleuro-pneumonia bill, the commissioner of agriculture is now besieged on all sides by applicants for the positions created by the bill. It is to be hoped that the commissioner will give those appointments his most careful consideration and attention. In its present form we have not much faith in the bill to do what the cattle industry demanded, but we do not want to see any but first-class men appointed to execute its provisions, that all the good there is in it may be brought out. We don't want any political fossils whose chief merit is the ability to run a caucus, but we want live, progressive business men identified with the great cattle interests of the country.—[Kansas City Drovers, News.
articles.summary: Clipped comment urging that appointments under the new pleuro-pneumonia law go to cattle men, not politicians.

articles.text: The following is the latest story from Benton: A 16-year old cowboy was driving a steer through Benton the other day. It got scared and dashed through the back door of a saloon and out of the front door on a dead run, followed by the daring boy on a pony. As the steer passed through he jumped clear over a table around which were four men engaged in a friendly game of poker, and when the men saw the boy following they dodged under the table, which made the pony's passage easier in leaping over it. Fortunately the doors were open and were wide enough both front and rear to make a good place of entrance and exit for the frightened steer.—[Tranchant.
articles.summary: Clipped story of a steer and a boy on a pony running through a Benton saloon.

articles.text: H. M. Sloan returned yesterday from the Shields river round-up. It is now working about Flathead and will be through in a week. Stock owners are well pleased with what the spring round-up has developed. The loss during the winter has been insingificant, calves are plentiful, cattle are rolling fat and the grass is more luxuriant than last year this time. The Shields river round-up, though it covers a great deal of ground includes only about 10,000 cattle, and these are principally owned by four concerns—Meyer Bros., Gianniss & Sons, Wright Bros. and Harvey & Treglone. There are many other stockmen in the valley, but they are but beginners and have comparatively small herds.—[Livingstone Enterprise.
articles.summary: Clipped Montana report on the Shields river round-up.

articles.text: The greatest sale of Short Horn cattle that has been made since that of B. B. Groom, several years ago, is reported from the stock farm of A. L. Hamilton, at Lexington, Ky., recently. The Kansas City Live Stock Indicator says. "The highest figures reached was $7,000 for a 2-year-old roan heifer, which was started by Mr. Swope at $3,000, followed by a bid of $4,000 from T. Corwin Anderson. G. L. Chrisman, of Independence, A. C. Briant, of Belton, and R. K. Thomson, of Slater, Mo., also purchased liberally of these, besides taking several of the other families. Counting the calves sold with dams as one animal there were 107 head sold, realizing a total of $87,450—an average of $817,20 per head, and of this large amount of money Missouri paid $35,585, Kansas $7,335, and Colorado $1,600.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped report of a record Short Horn sale at Lexington, Kentucky.

articles.text: Seldom has there been a more favorable season for stockmen than the present one. From all quarters come good reports of the round-ups and the loss of cattle is found to be very light notwithstanding what was called a hard winter. Grass is plenty and the stock is in good condition. It is true that from the mountains the calf crop is reported smaller than in the bad lands and whatever are the conditions of atmosphere or shelter that brings about that difference are yet to be explained. The bad lands affording the most shelter, are more favorable for wintering cattle, and hold the first place in the estimation of stock men. Where bulls have been scarce on the range there has been a consequent diminution in the number of calves, and the stock men of this section appreciating the need of good bulls have been investing heavily in sires this season, particularly in throughbred stock. A large increase of strong, healthy calves cannot be expected where the bulls are scarce or old, and the introduction of fine young males will make a great difference in the number of calves in succeeding round-ups.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped Yellowstone Journal report of a favorable season, light winter losses and heavy investment in bulls.

articles.text: While there is no likelihood of it ultimately displacing live cattle in the markets of the country, it must be admitted that the dressed meat trade is gradually extending its field of operations. Conducted with consummate tact, it is steadily widening its scope and gathering new patronage. The results of its growth are especially noticeable as affecting the trade in low grade cattle. It is becoming more difficult, as dressed beef becomes more widely introduced, to dispose of this grade of stock at fair relative prices to butchers who handle cheap stock. It is with these cattle that Chicago beef comes in direct competition. placing the butcher in an independent position as to supplying his wants with stock on the hoof. When he visits the retail market and finds the price of cattle beyond his views, he turns away to the Chicago warehouse and supplies himself at a low figure without the trouble of slaughtering. He can buy dressed beef at only a cent or two a pound above the cost of live cattle, and it is not strange that he takes advantage of this fact to stand off from advancing markets. Butchers in country towns are also handling increased quantities of Chicago beef, and are fitting up refrigerators for that purpose. This trade but slightly affects the sale of good cattle. There is a class of butchers, catering to the best city trade, who under all circumstances slaughter their own stock, and will continue to do so. This insures a continued good market for decent cattle, and ought to stimulate producers to greater pains in looking after the quality of what they grow. The tendency of the times is to run low grade stock out of the intermediate and eastern markets, and place choice cattle at a premium.—[National Stockman.
articles.summary: Clipped National Stockman article on the spread of the Chicago dressed-beef trade and its effect on low-grade cattle.

articles.summary: Mr. Barr drove in 200 beef steers for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.

articles.text: Some of as fine beef as a man need wish to see in any country was killed at the slaughter house this week.

articles.summary: Bernethy and Deadley's mule and horse trains arrived to load freight for Ryan & Son of Spearfish.

articles.text: Coleman & Brown's restaurant building is nearly completed, and they promise a good, square meal to the hungry in a few days.
articles.summary: Coleman & Brown's restaurant building is nearly completed.

articles.text: F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., accompanied by Fred McKinney, of Bismarck, paid Medora a flying visit last week.
articles.summary: F. B. Allen of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. and Fred McKinney of Bismarck made a brief visit to Medora.

articles.text: Roberts & Co. have removed their billiard hall from Little Missouri to Medora, occupying the down stairs of the new hall building.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. moved their billiard hall from Little Missouri to the new hall building in Medora.

articles.text: Thomas Matthews, inspector for the Wyoming Stock Association, and Al. Hockett, inspector for the East Montana Associatian, visited Medora this week.
articles.summary: Stock inspectors Thomas Matthews (Wyoming) and Al. Hockett (East Montana) visited Medora.

articles.text: Welf, from Deadwood, has opened out a good stock of notions, dry goods and gents' furnishing goods in a tent nearly opposite this office. He reports a fair trade.
articles.summary: Welf of Deadwood opened a dry goods and notions store in a tent opposite the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: P. D. Cravath, representing the Globe Oil Works, Minneapolis, was a visitor in our town on Sunday and left for Deadwood via the Medora route on Monday afternoon.
articles.summary: P. D. Cravath of the Globe Oil Works, Minneapolis, visited Medora and left for Deadwood by the Medora route.

articles.text: John O'Sullivan has his new barber shop and bath rooms completed, and now there is no excuse for any man going dirty, for a bath at John's rooms will only cost 50 cents.
articles.summary: John O'Sullivan completed his new barber shop and bath rooms; baths cost 50 cents.

articles.text: Nick Tiersey, a baker from Jamestown, Dak., arrived here on Wednesday. He is looking up a location for business, and expresses himself as well satisfied with the prospects of Medora. We predict he will stay with us.
articles.summary: Nick Tiersey, a Jamestown baker, arrived to look for a business location in Medora.

articles.text: Wm. Gay and C. W. Cowgill, of Spearfish, arrived here a few days since and took passage on Saturday's No. 1 for the Coeur d' Alene. Both of these gentlemen are old time Black Hillers and they pronounce the Medora route the chief.
articles.summary: Wm. Gay and C. W. Cowgill of Spearfish passed through Medora bound for the Coeur d'Alene.

articles.text: Lieut. Varnum, of the 7th cavalry, with a squad of men passed through last week enroute to Fort Meade via the Medora road. He is viewing the different routes from the Northern Pacific railroad to the Hills by order of the department commander.
articles.summary: Lieut. Varnum of the 7th Cavalry passed through Medora surveying routes from the Northern Pacific to the Black Hills.

articles.text: The Marquis de Mores returned from St. Paul on Friday night last, but left for the east again on Saturday morning. During his brief visit he expressed himself as well satisfied that the stages would be rolling to the hills from Medora in a short time.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès made a one-night visit from St. Paul and predicted the Medora-Black Hills stages would soon be running.

articles.text: A passenger on Monday's No. 1 let his curiosity overreach his discretion as the train was crossing the bridge. He leaned over so far, in order to see all he could, that his head collided with the bridge. Examination proved that the bridge suffered no damage. The passenger resumed his journey a sorer but a wiser man.
articles.summary: A passenger on the westbound train struck his head on the bridge while leaning out.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman will return to Minnesota in a few days to buy another lot of cattle. The satisfaction that they give is amply illustrated by the fact that a Glendive customer of theirs voluntarily counted in a number of calves at full yearling rates, while they are generally thrown in with the purchase.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman will go to Minnesota to buy more cattle.

articles.text: Roberts & Co. are busily engaged moving into the new hall building, which will be formaly opened on the 4th of July, when a grand ball will be given, including supper. An enjoyable time is assured to every one present, because the gentlemen having charge of the arrangements are among the most popular of our citizens.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. are moving into the new hall building, to be opened July 4 with a grand ball and supper.

articles.text: William Haley, who drove Pennell & Roberts team to the Hills, which was chartered by Messrs. Guild and Gallop, returned on Saturday evening last. Eight days was the time of the round trip, including a day and a half laying over, and with the same team the entire trip. This is as good time as the Pierre and Sidney coaches make with four horse stock and changes every 15 miles. The Medora route is the chief and no mistake.
articles.summary: William Haley returned from an eight-day round trip to the Black Hills with a Pennell & Roberts team chartered by Guild and Gallop.

articles.text: On Tuesday evening about dark three strangers were observed loafing around some saddled horses hitched in front of the Hotel de Mores. They apparently had the intention of appropriating some of the animals, but the appearance of George Fitzgerald frustrated their evil designs. This town has, we are pleased to say, so far been neglected by horse thieves, much to the delight of owners of horse flesh; but another break like that made by these strangers and instead of stealing horses it is buckshot the thieves are more likely to carry off.
articles.summary: Three strangers apparently trying to steal horses in front of the Hotel de Mores were scared off by George Fitzgerald.

articles.text: A. T. Packard, the editor of the Cow Boy, started on Monday last for Deadwood in company with P. D. Cravath, representative of the Globe Oil Works at Minneapolis. They took one of Pennell & Roberts' boss mule teams and expect to be gone about ten days. If the rain and hail storm of Monday night reached them in camp we can imagine how merry a party they were. It is only necessary to say they had one slicker between three of them for the reader to imagine their feelings. The editor's absence will account for any deficiency in the quantity or quality of reading matter in the Cow Boy this week.
articles.summary: Editor A. T. Packard left for Deadwood with P. D. Cravath by mule team, expecting to be gone ten days; a rain and hail storm struck Monday night.

articles.text: The editor, Rassie Deffebach and a friend of the editor's from the east, will always remember last Sunday as one of their red letter days. A magnificent day, a magnificent ride, a view of some of the most wierd and imposing scenery of the Bad Lands, and to crown it all the best of dinners at Wadsworth's ranch served by the most hospitable of ladies, ought certainly to make a day full of pleasure. Mrs. Wadsworth and Mrs. McGregor will always be remembered with most kindly feeling by their visitors. If any hungry citizens of Medora want a good dinner and a drink of the best buttermilk in the Bad Lands we advise them to make a visit to Wadsworth's ranch; but we warn them to stick to the beaten road and not attempt a will o' the wisp jaunt across coolies and perpendicular buttes, where only the fine Italian hand of Rassie Deffebach or a miracle could take them through. If any one aspires to fame as an equestrian acrobat, let him follow our trail from the lower plateau to the higher plateau above Metzen's ranch. Everybody said it couldn't be done, but we did it.
articles.summary: The editor, Rassie Deffebach and an eastern friend rode through the Bad Lands to dinner at Wadsworth's ranch, hosted by Mrs. Wadsworth and Mrs. McGregor.

articles.text:
From the Mandan Pioneer of June 30 we clip the following items:

Seventy-seven cars of live stock and about forty cars of freight were temporarily delayed at Mandan by the Marmot washout.

The washout near Marmot will be fully repaired to-day, so as to admit of the passage of trains.

Assistant Superintendent Green will start out to-morrow to pay off on the Missouri division.
articles.summary: Mandan Pioneer items on the Marmot washout that held up 77 cars of live stock and 40 of freight, and on the Missouri division pay car.

articles.text: Sidney Dillon has a herd of about 8,000 cattle on the trail from North Platte to Powder river. The high water has detained them a little, but they will get through in good season.
articles.summary: Sidney Dillon's herd of about 8,000 cattle is on the trail from North Platte to Powder river.

articles.text: The weather for the past week for the most part has been clear, warm and pleasant. The grass is everywhere growing rapidly and the feed is all that could be desired. The abundant rains of the past six weeks were fortunat[illegible] from this time on we can get along without rain. The grass has all the start it needs. Dry weather now will cure it for winter feed.
articles.summary: The week's weather was clear, warm and pleasant, and the grass is growing well after six weeks of rain.

articles.text: Mrs. Langtry, while here recently was driven out to see the company's ranch by Manager Oelrich. She was delighted with the trip in the "Tally Ho," and made careful investigation of the ranch and how the business was managed. The result is that she concluded to invest a large amount of money in the cattle business of this country. She has an eye to business and her venture will prove a grand success.—[Northwestern Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped Northwestern Live Stock Journal item that Mrs. Langtry visited a company ranch with Manager Oelrich and decided to invest in cattle.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Cow Boy urges Medora be made the Black Hills freight point
events.summary: The Cow Boy argued that the Northern Pacific should contract with a single forwarding company and make Medora the only starting point on the line for Black Hills freight, put at 15,000,000 pounds this year.
events.excerpt: the importance of doing all in our power to make Medora a permanent starting point for Black Hills freight presents itself.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Col. G. A. Pierce appointed governor of Dakota
events.summary: Quoting the Bismarck Journal, the paper reported that Col. G. A. Pierce of Chicago had been appointed governor of Dakota in place of Ordway, and the editor predicted Pierce would be the territory's best governor.
events.excerpt: Col. G. A. Pierce, of Chicago, has been appointed governor of Dakota, vice Ordway, whose term has expired.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Editor rebuts report that Yellowstone ranges are closed to newcomers
events.summary: Answering a report that Yellowstone ranchers would bar newcomers from the round-up, the editor wrote that the Bad Lands ranges were not crowded and offered water, shelter and feed year round.
events.excerpt: the Bad Lands ranges are not, and to-day no better cattle country can be found in the United States than in these ranges

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Cattle firms offer $250 reward against grass fires
events.summary: The N. P. Ref. Car Co., Continental Cattle Co., Hughes & Simpson, Dorr Clark, Clark & Plum, Dickey Bros. and E. G. Paddock offered $250 for information leading to the arrest of anyone setting grass fires in Western Dakota's cattle sections.
events.excerpt: The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Reward offered for horses missing from Week's ranche
events.summary: Culbertson & Weeks of Keith offered $40 for the return of a horse and three ponies to Week's ranche on Beaver creek, and $20 for information leading to their recovery.
events.excerpt: Forty dollars will be paid for the return to Week's ranche, Beaver creek, Montana, of the following stock

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Fargo Argus notes the Cow Boy's page of brands
events.summary: The Cow Boy reprinted a Fargo Argus note that one page of the paper carried thirty-one brand announcements, nearly all headquartered at Medora, as a sign of Dakota becoming stock country.
events.excerpt: One page contains the announcement of thirty-one brands, ranges, ear mark and vint, and the headquarters of nearly all these ranges are at Medora

events.date_basis: "next week" after Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Coal mine to start up
events.summary: The paper reported the coal mine would start up the following week.
events.excerpt: The coal mine will start up next week.

events.date_basis: "Friday last" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: C. W. Sleeper leaves for the east
events.summary: C. W. Sleeper left for the east.
events.excerpt: C. W. Sleeper left for the east on Friday last.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Markley and McArthur outfits arrive
events.summary: The outfits of Jim Markley and Dan McArthur arrived.
events.excerpt: Jim Markley's and Dan McArthur's outfits arrived last Saturday.

events.date_basis: "during the past week" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Black Hills freight arrives by rail
events.summary: Several carloads of Black Hills freight arrived at Medora during the week.
events.excerpt: Several cars loaded with Black Hills freight have arrived during the past week.

events.date_basis: "Monday last" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Barr drives in 200 beef steers for the N. P. Ref. Car Co.
events.summary: Mr. Barr drove in 200 head of fine beef steers for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.
events.excerpt: Mr. Barr drove in 200 head of fine beef steers on Monday last, for the N. P. Ref. Car Co.

events.date_basis: "this week", week ending Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Fine beef killed at the slaughter house
events.summary: The paper reported that some very fine beef was killed at the slaughter house this week.
events.excerpt: Some of as fine beef as a man need wish to see in any country was killed at the slaughter house this week.

events.date_basis: "this week", week ending Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Bernethy and Deadley freight trains arrive
events.summary: Bernethy and Deadley's mule and horse trains pulled in and were to load freight for Ryan & Son of Spearfish.
events.excerpt: They will load with freight for Ryan & Son, Spearfish.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Coleman & Brown's restaurant nearly done
events.summary: Coleman & Brown's restaurant building was nearly completed, with meals promised in a few days.
events.excerpt: Coleman & Brown's restaurant building is nearly completed, and they promise a good, square meal to the hungry in a few days.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 3 Jul 1884 (week of Mon 23 Jun)
events.title: F. B. Allen and Fred McKinney visit Medora
events.summary: F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., and Fred McKinney of Bismarck paid Medora a brief visit.
events.excerpt: F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., accompanied by Fred McKinney, of Bismarck, paid Medora a flying visit last week.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Roberts & Co. move billiard hall to Medora
events.summary: Roberts & Co. moved their billiard hall from Little Missouri to the ground floor of the new hall building in Medora.
events.excerpt: Roberts & Co. have removed their billiard hall from Little Missouri to Medora, occupying the down stairs of the new hall building.

events.date_basis: "this week", week ending Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Stock association inspectors visit Medora
events.summary: Thomas Matthews, inspector for the Wyoming Stock Association, and Al. Hockett, inspector for the East Montana Association, visited Medora.
events.excerpt: Thomas Matthews, inspector for the Wyoming Stock Association, and Al. Hockett, inspector for the East Montana Associatian, visited Medora this week.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Welf opens tent store opposite the Cow Boy office
events.summary: Welf of Deadwood opened a stock of notions, dry goods and gents' furnishings in a tent nearly opposite the Cow Boy office, and reported fair trade.
events.excerpt: Welf, from Deadwood, has opened out a good stock of notions, dry goods and gents' furnishing goods in a tent nearly opposite this office.

events.date_basis: "Sunday" before Thu 3 Jul 1884; left "Monday" 30 Jun
events.title: P. D. Cravath visits and leaves for Deadwood
events.summary: P. D. Cravath of the Globe Oil Works, Minneapolis, visited Medora on Sunday and left for Deadwood via the Medora route on Monday afternoon.
events.excerpt: was a visitor in our town on Sunday and left for Deadwood via the Medora route on Monday afternoon.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: John O'Sullivan opens barber shop and bath rooms
events.summary: John O'Sullivan completed his new barber shop and bath rooms, where a bath cost 50 cents.
events.excerpt: a bath at John's rooms will only cost 50 cents.

events.date_basis: "Wednesday" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Jamestown baker Nick Tiersey arrives
events.summary: Nick Tiersey, a baker from Jamestown, arrived looking for a business location and was well satisfied with Medora's prospects.
events.excerpt: Nick Tiersey, a baker from Jamestown, Dak., arrived here on Wednesday.

events.date_basis: "Saturday's No. 1" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Spearfish men take train for the Coeur d'Alene
events.summary: Wm. Gay and C. W. Cowgill of Spearfish, old-time Black Hillers, arrived a few days earlier and took the westbound No. 1 for the Coeur d'Alene, calling the Medora route the chief.
events.excerpt: Both of these gentlemen are old time Black Hillers and they pronounce the Medora route the chief.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 3 Jul 1884 (week of Mon 23 Jun)
events.title: Lieut. Varnum surveys the Medora road to Fort Meade
events.summary: Lieut. Varnum of the 7th Cavalry passed through with a squad of men on the way to Fort Meade by the Medora road, examining routes from the Northern Pacific to the Black Hills by order of the department commander.
events.excerpt: He is viewing the different routes from the Northern Pacific railroad to the Hills by order of the department commander.

events.date_basis: "Friday night last" before Thu 3 Jul 1884; left Saturday 28 Jun
events.title: Marquis de Morès makes brief visit, predicts stages soon running
events.summary: The Marquis de Morès returned from St. Paul on Friday night and left for the east Saturday morning, saying he was satisfied the stages to the Hills would soon be rolling from Medora.
events.excerpt: During his brief visit he expressed himself as well satisfied that the stages would be rolling to the hills from Medora in a short time.

events.date_basis: "Monday's No. 1" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Train passenger strikes head on bridge
events.summary: A passenger on the westbound No. 1 leaned out so far as the train crossed the bridge that his head struck it; the paper joked that the bridge was undamaged.
events.excerpt: Examination proved that the bridge suffered no damage.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman to buy cattle in Minnesota
events.summary: Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman planned to return to Minnesota in a few days to buy another lot of cattle.
events.excerpt: Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman will return to Minnesota in a few days to buy another lot of cattle.

events.date_basis: "the 4th of July" 1884
events.title: Grand ball to open new hall building on the Fourth
events.summary: Roberts & Co. were moving into the new hall building, to be formally opened on the Fourth of July with a grand ball and supper.
events.excerpt: which will be formaly opened on the 4th of July, when a grand ball will be given, including supper.

events.date_basis: "Saturday evening last" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Haley returns from eight-day round trip to the Hills
events.summary: William Haley returned from driving a Pennell & Roberts team, chartered by Guild and Gallop, to the Black Hills and back in eight days with the same team, which the paper said matched the Pierre and Sidney coaches.
events.excerpt: Eight days was the time of the round trip, including a day and a half laying over, and with the same team the entire trip.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday evening" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Would-be horse thieves frustrated at Hotel de Mores
events.summary: Three strangers loafing around saddled horses in front of the Hotel de Mores apparently meant to steal them but were frustrated by George Fitzgerald; the paper warned that the next thieves would more likely carry off buckshot.
events.excerpt: instead of stealing horses it is buckshot the thieves are more likely to carry off.

events.date_basis: "Monday last" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Packard leaves for Deadwood by mule team
events.summary: Editor A. T. Packard set out for Deadwood with P. D. Cravath of the Globe Oil Works, using a Pennell & Roberts mule team, expecting to be gone about ten days; the paper blamed his absence for any thinness in the issue.
events.excerpt: A. T. Packard, the editor of the Cow Boy, started on Monday last for Deadwood in company with P. D. Cravath

events.date_basis: "Monday night" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Rain and hail storm Monday night
events.summary: The paper mentioned a rain and hail storm on Monday night, wondering whether it caught the editor's party in camp with one slicker among three men.
events.excerpt: If the rain and hail storm of Monday night reached them in camp we can imagine how merry a party they were.

events.date_basis: "last Sunday" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Editor's Bad Lands ride and dinner at Wadsworth's ranch
events.summary: The editor, Rassie Deffebach and an eastern friend rode through the Bad Lands to dinner at Wadsworth's ranch, hosted by Mrs. Wadsworth and Mrs. McGregor, then climbed from the lower to the higher plateau above Metzen's ranch.
events.excerpt: the best of dinners at Wadsworth's ranch served by the most hospitable of ladies

events.date_basis: Mandan Pioneer of Mon 30 Jun 1884 reports washout already in place; repair "to-day" 30 Jun
events.title: Marmot washout delays stock and freight trains
events.summary: Quoting the Mandan Pioneer of June 30, the paper reported that seventy-seven cars of live stock and about forty of freight were held at Mandan by a washout near Marmot, to be repaired that day.
events.excerpt: Seventy-seven cars of live stock and about forty cars of freight were temporarily delayed at Mandan by the Marmot washout.

events.date_basis: "for the past week" before Thu 3 Jul 1884
events.title: Clear, warm week and strong grass
events.summary: The week's weather was mostly clear, warm and pleasant; after six weeks of abundant rain the grass was growing rapidly, and dry weather would now cure it for winter feed.
events.excerpt: The weather for the past week for the most part has been clear, warm and pleasant.
